Presentation of Christ
prez-uhn-TAY-shuhn uhv KRYST
proper noun
The bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple to be presented to the Lord, forty days after His birth (Luke 2:22–38).

📖 Biblical Definition

The presentation of Christ is the bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple in Jerusalem, forty days after His birth, that He might be presented to the Lord according to the law of Moses, and that His mother might offer the appointed sacrifice of purification—a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, the offering of the poor. The scene is rich with gospel light. The aged and devout Simeon, to whom it had been revealed that he should not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ, took the child in his arms and blessed God: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. He warned Mary that this child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and that a sword should pierce through her own soul. Anna the prophetess, a widow of great age who departed not from the temple, gave thanks likewise and spoke of Him to all that looked for redemption in Jerusalem. The dictionary reads the presentation of Christ as the meeting of the Old Covenant’s waiting saints with the Saviour come at last: the firstborn presented to the Lord, the law fulfilled, and the long-expected salvation, prepared for both Gentile and Jew, beheld and confessed by Simeon and Anna.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The bringing of the infant Jesus to the temple forty days after His birth; the meeting with Simeon and Anna, who beheld the salvation prepared—a light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

📖 Key Scripture

Luk 2:22 — "And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord;"

Luk 2:30 — "For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,"

Luk 2:32 — "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel."

Luk 2:38 — "And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the feast is overlaid with Marian devotion; the scene’s glory is the Saviour beheld, the salvation prepared for Gentile and Jew.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The accretion to set aside is the medieval overlaying of this scene with Marian devotion—the feast kept as the “Purification of the Blessed Virgin,” with attention bent toward the mother rather than the Son. But Luke’s account fixes every eye on the child: it is Christ who is presented to the Lord, Christ whom Simeon beheld as the salvation of God, Christ who is the light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. Mary’s purification offering is the offering of the poor, and Simeon’s word to her foretells a sword through her own soul—she is a humble worshipper in the scene, not its object.

The principle to recover is the Saviour beheld by the waiting saints. The presentation gathers up the longing of the Old Covenant: Simeon, who waited for the consolation of Israel, and Anna, who spoke of Him to all that looked for redemption, are the faithful remnant whose eyes at last see the salvation of God. The infant fulfills the law as the firstborn presented to the Lord, and is shown to be the salvation prepared before the face of all people—a light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. The glory of the scene is wholly Christ’s.
